1.1.name: Science Process Skills
1.1.revision: Science process skills are basic skills that help scientists carry out investigations. These include observing (using senses to gather information), classifying (grouping objects based on characteristics), measuring (using tools to obtain quantitative data), predicting (making educated guesses about outcomes), and communicating (sharing findings through text, tables, or charts). These skills form the foundation of all scientific work.

questions.q: Which science process skill involves using your senses to describe the colour, shape, and texture of an object?

Ali uses a stopwatch to record how long it takes for sugar to dissolve in water. Which skill is he demonstrating?
After noticing dark clouds in the sky, Amin says, 'I think it will rain this evening.' Which science process skill is he using?
Presenting data from an experiment using a bar chart is an example of which science process skill?
A student notices that a metal spoon feels colder than a wooden spoon at the same temperature. Which skill is being used?

1.2.name: Manipulative Skills
1.2.revision: Manipulative skills involve the proper use of scientific apparatus and materials in experiments. These include using and handling science apparatus correctly (like test tubes, beakers, and thermometers), handling specimens carefully (like plants and insects), drawing specimens and apparatus accurately, and cleaning and storing equipment properly after use. Good manipulative skills ensure safety and accurate results in experiments.

a: Use forceps gently and keep it moist

questions.q: Why should you wear safety goggles during a science experiment?
a: To protect your eyes from splashes or flying objects

1.3.name: Applying Scientific Skills
1.3.revision: Applying scientific skills means using science process skills and manipulative skills together to design and carry out simple experiments. This includes identifying problems, making hypotheses, planning fair tests by controlling variables, observing and recording data, interpreting results, and drawing conclusions. A fair test ensures that only one variable is changed while others are kept constant, so results are reliable.

2.1.name: Human Skeleton
2.1.revision: The human skeleton is made up of bones that support the body, protect internal organs, and allow movement. The skeleton has over 200 bones. The skull protects the brain, the rib cage protects the heart and lungs, and the backbone (spine) supports the body and protects the spinal cord. Bones are connected at joints and work with muscles to help us move.

questions.q: What is the main function of the human skeleton?
a: To support the body, protect organs, and help movement

2.2.name: Muscles
2.2.revision: Muscles are tissues that contract (shorten) and relax (lengthen) to produce movement. There are three types of muscles: skeletal muscles (attached to bones, voluntary movement), smooth muscles (found in organs like stomach, involuntary), and cardiac muscle (found in the heart, involuntary). Muscles often work in pairs — one muscle contracts while the other relaxes, such as the biceps and triceps in the arm.

2.3.name: Joints
2.3.revision: A joint is where two or more bones meet. Different types of joints allow different kinds of movement. Hinge joints (like elbow and knee) allow movement in one direction like a door hinge. Ball-and-socket joints (like shoulder and hip) allow movement in many directions. Fixed joints (like the skull bones) do not allow any movement. Joints help our body move smoothly.

2.4.name: Taking Care of Our Body
2.4.revision: Taking care of our body involves maintaining good posture, exercising regularly, eating a balanced diet, and getting enough rest. Good posture (standing and sitting straight) prevents back pain and keeps the skeleton properly aligned. Regular exercise strengthens muscles and bones. Stretching before exercise helps prevent injuries. A balanced diet with calcium and vitamin D keeps bones strong.

a: Keeping your back straight when sitting or standing

3.1.name: Food Preservation Methods
3.1.revision: Food preservation methods help keep food from spoiling for longer periods. Common methods include drying (removing water from food like fish and fruits), freezing (keeping food at very low temperatures), boiling (heating food to kill bacteria), salting (adding salt to draw out moisture), pickling (soaking food in vinegar or salt solution), and canning (sealing food in airtight containers after heating). Each method prevents the growth of microorganisms that cause spoilage.

3.2.name: Why Food Needs to be Preserved
3.2.revision: Food needs to be preserved to prevent spoilage caused by microorganisms like bacteria, mould, and yeast. These microorganisms need food, water, warmth, and air to grow and reproduce. Spoiled food becomes rotten, changes colour and smell, and can cause food poisoning if eaten. Preserving food also extends its shelf life, reduces waste, and allows us to enjoy seasonal food all year round.

3.3.name: Human Digestive System
3.3.revision: The human digestive system breaks down food into nutrients that the body can absorb and use. Digestion begins in the mouth where teeth chew food and saliva starts breaking it down. The food then travels down the oesophagus (food pipe) to the stomach, where digestive juices break it down further. The small intestine absorbs nutrients into the blood, and the large intestine absorbs water before waste is removed from the body.

4.1.name: Electrical Circuits
4.1.revision: An electrical circuit is a complete path through which electric current flows. A simple circuit consists of a source of electricity (like a battery or cell), wires (to carry the current), a load (like a bulb that uses the electricity), and often a switch (to control the flow). For current to flow, the circuit must be complete — there must be no gaps in the path. When the switch is closed (on), the circuit is complete and the bulb lights up.

a: The circuit is broken and the bulb does not light up

a: To provide the energy for current to flow

a: Connect the components and carry electric current

a: There is a loose connection or gap in the circuit

4.2.name: Series and Parallel Circuits
4.2.revision: In a series circuit, components are connected one after another in a single path. If one bulb blows, all bulbs go out. In a parallel circuit, components are connected in separate branches. If one bulb blows, the others stay lit. Bulbs in a parallel circuit are brighter than bulbs in a series circuit with the same number of bulbs because each bulb gets the full voltage. Parallel circuits are used in home wiring.

questions.q: In a series circuit with two bulbs, what happens if one bulb blows?
a: The other bulb also goes out

4.3.name: Conductors and Insulators
4.3.revision: Conductors are materials that allow electric current to flow through them easily. Most metals like copper, iron, and aluminium are good conductors of electricity. Insulators are materials that do not allow electric current to flow through them easily. Examples include rubber, plastic, wood, glass, and dry cloth. Conductors are used for wires, while insulators are used as covers or handles to protect us from electric shocks.

4.4.name: Safety with Electricity
4.4.revision: Electricity can be dangerous if not handled properly. Safety rules include: never touch electrical appliances with wet hands, never stick objects into sockets, do not overload sockets with too many plugs, keep electrical appliances away from water, do not pull the cord to unplug an appliance, and ask an adult to fix damaged wires. Following these rules prevents electric shocks, fires, and injuries.

5.1.name: Sources of Light
5.1.revision: Light sources can be natural or artificial. Natural light sources include the Sun, stars, fireflies, and lightning. Artificial light sources are made by humans and include torches, lamps, candles, light bulbs, and televisions. Objects like the Moon and mirrors are not light sources — they only reflect light from other sources. Light is a form of energy that allows us to see things.

5.2.name: Light Travels in a Straight Line
5.2.revision: Light travels in straight lines. This property explains why shadows form — when an opaque object blocks the path of light, it creates a dark area (shadow) behind the object. The shape and size of a shadow depend on the position of the light source and the distance between the object and the screen. When the light source is closer, the shadow is bigger. When the source is directly above, the shadow is short.

5.3.name: Reflection of Light
5.3.revision: Reflection occurs when light bounces off a surface. Smooth, shiny surfaces like mirrors reflect light well and produce clear images. Rough surfaces scatter light in many directions, so they do not form clear images. We see objects because light reflects off them into our eyes. A periscope uses two mirrors to reflect light, allowing you to see over obstacles. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

5.4.name: Refraction of Light
5.4.revision: Refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one transparent medium to another at an angle, such as from air into water. This happens because light travels at different speeds in different materials. Refraction explains why a straw in a glass of water appears bent or broken, and why fish in a pond appear closer to the surface than they really are. Lenses use refraction to focus light.

6.1.name: Sources of Heat
6.1.revision: Heat is a form of energy that makes things warmer. Heat comes from various sources. The Sun is the main natural source of heat on Earth. Other heat sources include friction (rubbing hands together), electricity (flowing through a wire or appliance), burning (fire, candles), and chemical reactions. Heat energy can be used for cooking, warming ourselves, drying clothes, and generating electricity.

6.2.name: Heat Transfer
6.2.revision: Heat can be transferred in three ways: conduction, convection, and radiation. Conduction is the transfer of heat through solids by direct contact between particles — for example, a metal spoon gets hot when placed in hot soup. Convection is the transfer of heat through liquids and gases by the movement of particles — hot water rises and cool water sinks. Radiation is the transfer of heat through empty space without needing a medium — the Sun's heat reaches Earth through radiation.

6.3.name: Conductors and Insulators of Heat
6.3.revision: Heat conductors are materials that allow heat to pass through them easily. Metals like iron, copper, and aluminium are good heat conductors. Heat insulators are materials that do not allow heat to pass through them easily. Wood, plastic, rubber, cloth, and air are good heat insulators. Cookware is made of metal (good conductor) with plastic or wooden handles (good insulator) to protect our hands from burns.

6.4.name: Effects of Heat
6.4.revision: Heat causes matter to expand (increase in size) when heated and contract (decrease in size) when cooled. This is called thermal expansion and contraction. For example, railway tracks have gaps to allow for expansion on hot days. A thermometer works because the liquid inside expands when heated and contracts when cooled. Balloons may burst in hot weather because the air inside expands. Understanding these effects helps us design things that can handle temperature changes.

7.1.name: States of Matter
7.1.revision: Matter exists in three main states: solid, liquid, and gas. Solids have a fixed shape and volume, and their particles are packed closely together in a fixed arrangement. Liquids have a fixed volume but no fixed shape — they take the shape of their container, and their particles are loosely packed. Gases have no fixed shape or volume — they spread to fill any container, and their particles are far apart and move freely. Each state has distinct properties.

7.2.name: Changes in State
7.2.revision: Matter can change from one state to another when heat is added or removed. Melting is the change from solid to liquid (ice melts into water when heated). Freezing is the change from liquid to solid (water freezes into ice when cooled). Evaporation is the change from liquid to gas (water turns into water vapour when heated). Condensation is the change from gas to liquid (water vapour turns into water droplets when cooled). These are physical changes — no new substances are formed.

7.3.name: Water Cycle
7.3.revision: The water cycle is the continuous movement of water between the Earth's surface and the atmosphere. The Sun's heat causes water from oceans, rivers, and lakes to evaporate and turn into water vapour (evaporation). The water vapour rises, cools, and condenses into tiny water droplets that form clouds (condensation). When the droplets become heavy, they fall back to Earth as rain, snow, or hail (precipitation). The water cycle ensures that Earth has a continuous supply of fresh water.

8.1.name: Life Cycle of Animals
8.1.revision: Animals go through different stages during their lives. A butterfly undergoes complete metamorphosis with four stages: egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa (chrysalis), and adult butterfly. A frog's life cycle includes: egg, tadpole (breathes through gills, has a tail), froglet (develops legs, tail shrinks), and adult frog (breathes through lungs and skin). A mosquito's life cycle includes: egg, larva (wriggler), pupa (tumbler), and adult mosquito. Some animals undergo incomplete metamorphosis where the young look like small adults.

8.2.name: Life Cycle of Plants
8.2.revision: Plants also go through a life cycle. It begins with germination, where a seed absorbs water and a root and shoot emerge. The seedling grows into a mature plant with leaves, stems, and roots. The mature plant produces flowers, which are the reproductive parts. Flowers develop into fruits that contain seeds. The seeds are dispersed and when they land in suitable conditions, a new life cycle begins. Each part of the plant has a special function in the life cycle.

8.3.name: Comparing Life Cycles
8.3.revision: Different animals and plants have different life cycles. Some animals, like butterflies and frogs, undergo metamorphosis where their body shape changes dramatically between stages. Others, like chickens and cats, are born looking like smaller versions of adults and grow gradually. Some life cycles are short (butterfly: a few weeks) while others are long (humans: many decades). Plants also vary — some complete their life cycle in one year (annuals), others live for many years (perennials). Each life cycle is adapted to the organism's environment.

9.1.name: The Moon
9.1.revision: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite. It orbits Earth approximately once every 29.5 days. The Moon does not produce its own light — it reflects light from the Sun. The surface of the Moon has craters (formed by meteor impacts), mountains, and flat areas called maria (seas). The Moon goes through phases as seen from Earth: new Moon (not visible), crescent Moon, half Moon (first quarter), gibbous Moon, full Moon (completely lit), and then back through the same phases in reverse. These phases depend on the position of the Moon relative to the Sun and Earth.

9.2.name: Constellations
9.2.revision: Constellations are patterns of stars in the night sky that form recognisable shapes. Different constellations are visible at different times of the year and from different locations on Earth. Well-known constellations include Orion (the Hunter, with three stars in a line forming a belt), the Big Dipper (a ladle-shaped group of seven stars in the constellation Ursa Major), and the Southern Cross (Crux, a cross-shaped constellation visible in the Southern Hemisphere). Ancient civilisations used constellations for navigation and storytelling.

9.3.name: Using Constellations
9.3.revision: Constellations have been used by people for thousands of years to find directions, especially by sailors and travellers. In the Northern Hemisphere, the North Star (Polaris) is located using the Big Dipper and always points north. In the Southern Hemisphere, the Southern Cross is used to find the direction south. Constellations were also used by farmers to know when to plant crops and by sailors to navigate across oceans at night. Today, constellations help astronomers locate objects in the sky.

10.1.name: Types of Natural Disasters
10.1.revision: Natural disasters are extreme events caused by natural processes of the Earth. Types include floods (overflow of water onto normally dry land), landslides (movement of rock or soil down a slope), earthquakes (shaking of the ground caused by tectonic plate movements), tsunamis (large ocean waves caused by underwater earthquakes or volcanic eruptions), and volcanic eruptions (explosion of lava, ash, and gases from a volcano). Each type of disaster has different causes and effects on people and the environment.

10.2.name: Causes of Natural Disasters
10.2.revision: Natural disasters are caused by natural processes, but human activities can also increase their frequency or severity. Earthquakes are caused by movements of tectonic plates. Floods can be caused by heavy rainfall, overflowing rivers, or human activities like deforestation and poor drainage. Landslides are caused by heavy rain on steep slopes, especially where trees have been removed. Tsunamis are triggered by underwater earthquakes or volcanic eruptions. Volcanic eruptions happen when magma from inside the Earth rises to the surface. Climate change is increasing the frequency of some natural disasters like floods and droughts.

10.3.name: Safety During Natural Disasters
10.3.revision: Being prepared for natural disasters can save lives. Before a disaster, you should prepare an emergency kit with food, water, medicine, torch, and first aid supplies, and know evacuation routes. During an earthquake, drop, cover, and hold on under a sturdy table. During a flood, move to higher ground and never walk or swim in floodwater. During a tsunami warning, move immediately to high ground. During a volcanic eruption, cover your mouth and nose with a mask or cloth and follow evacuation orders. Always listen to official warnings and instructions from authorities.
